text:
Introduction
Welcome! On this website, you will be able to find all materials needed for the successful completion of your thesis.
This website was created by me, your supervisor - Lucija Sorić. It exists to simplify our workflows and offer a centralized platform that is easy to find (it is just one link!) and easy to share (still just one link!).
Some parts of this website are static, and unlikely to undergo major change. For example, contact details will always remain the same.
Other aspects, such as research materials, instructions, meeting summaries, and others, will be updated at the appropriate time. The Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) section will be updated regularly, as more questions come in. This way, I am trying to ensure all of you can benefit from shared information, even if you were not the one to ask it.
Thanks for reading and looking forward to working with you!

title: Thesis Process
text:
Here, you can find all the information and materials needed to complete different sections of your thesis.
I will also share some tips for each aspect, as well as some general writing guidelines. However, do consult the thesis syllabus/student guide (click here) in order to ensure your sections are also in line with graded components.

title: 1  Preparation
text:
Project Description: Fall 26/27
Our first meeting will be in the second week of September. In order for me to be able to plan the meeting and to ensure we are on track, I have prepared a to-do list of things you needed to do prior to our meeting.
Who Trusts Science? Personality, Politics, and Attitudes toward Science
Public trust in science shapes how people respond to scientific evidence and policy, but trust levels vary systematically by group. This is particularly true for those with certain political attitudes and worldviews (Gligorić et al., 2025). Gender, ethnicity, socioeconomic status and personality traits have also been identified as factors influencing levels of trust and attitudes towards science (Druckman et al., 2025; Fuglsang, 2024). Given ongoing societal changes such as the rise of the use of artificial agents, climate change, and political polarization, understanding what shapes individuals’ responsiveness to science is increasingly important, since science informs the policies addressing these changes.
Students will collect survey-based data using validated self-report instruments, collecting data collaboratively with their group. Each student will select a subset of variables to test their own hypothesis about individual differences and trust in science.
Variables included: age, gender, political beliefs (various questionnaires), attitudes towards science (various questionnaires).
Variables that can be added in case of interest: attitudes towards women (e.g., manosphere beliefs), socioeconomic status, self-reported technology/artificial intelligence use, etc.

title: 2  Proposal
text:
Why do I need a research proposal?
A research proposal is one of the most important parts of a research project. It formulates a theoretical background and a specific plan you aim to follow.
Every project, academic or not, needs a plan. A research proposal is essentially a formalized, written plan of your future steps.
When doing academic research, there are often many roads you can take - or many ways a project can go. This is true for any project, too. For example, if you want to paint a wall, you can choose between many colors! However, some of these options are more logical than others. Maybe you do not like some of the colors, maybe some colors are not available, maybe some colors clash with the furniture you own… In order to move forward with your project you have to make some decisions (i.e., choose a color), and you have to be able to explain this decision (at least to yourself).
A research proposal helps you think ahead since it asks you to make certain decisions prior to starting. By completing this step, you will save your future self a lot of time.

title: 2  Proposal
section: How do I write a research proposal?
text:
How do I write a research proposal?

Read the literature previously shared with you.
Find a set of variables you are genuinely interested in exploring.
Think about the measures you can use to research these variables. Refer to the planned questionnaires and scales.
Do not plan to mix questionnaires into one variable, and do not split them up unless you have a good reason (or a published paper provided a good argument for it).
Formulate a research question and hypotheses with this set of variables.
Write all the plans up, together with all other parts of the proposal.

In practice, it takes a few tries to complete the step 5. It is likely that you will have to go through the steps 2-5 multiple times, each time reading more literature in order to improve your research question. This is normal and part of the process.

title: 2  Proposal
section: What do I include in a research proposal?
text:
What do I include in a research proposal?
Please only follow the below guidelines when writing your proposal. The word count is an estimate, and you are welcome to go a bit over if needed. However, try to be as concise as possible while not losing important information.
There is no minimum or maximum amount of citations you should include. However, it is unlikely for the proposal to be written according to the guidelines without a substantial amount of citations.

Scientific background (~200 words)
Briefly describe the current state of the literature that led to your project idea. Provide definitions/descriptions of relevant concepts. Give more attention to a few key studies that directly address your research question.


Objectives & implications (~200 words)
Clearly describe the aims of your project. Describe how your research complements the current literature, or how it fits a gap. Argue why this is important to do. You can argue for real-life relevance, too, not just for scientific benefit. These should all follow from the previously described background. You can include your research question here.


Hypotheses (as many words as needed)
Formulate clear, specific hypotheses based on your research question. You can have multiple hypotheses, but you can also have just one - it is fully dependent on your question. For each hypothesis, state an expectation, explain how this expectation follows from previous literature.
An expectation needs to be specific - it is not enough to state you expect something to be different.
Example of a bad expectation:
I hypothesize I will/expect to find a difference in trust in science between the two groups.
Example of a good expectation:
I hypothesize I will/expect to find lower scores (this specifies the difference) on questionnaires measuring beliefs in science (this specifies the variable and the measure) in men compared to women (this specifies the direction of difference).*
* This would be even better if you state the exact difference you expect. E.g., you expect to find scores that are at least 5 points lower. Remember: be as specific as possible.


Methods (~700 words)
For each section, provide a clear description and motivation for the choice made.

Design
Briefly address the study design (e.g., cross-sectional, longitudinal). State what type of measures will be used (e.g., self-reports) and where data collection will take place (e.g., online).


Participants
Indicate the expected characteristics of the sample, namely mention the sample size and the population you want to sample. The population will most likely be undergraduate students at Tilburg University. However, in case of availability, the population could focus on other groups (e.g., adults, specific genders, etc.). This is to be determined.


Measures
Describe each variable of your study, how it is measured, and what the expected output of the measure will be (e.g., a singular number, a score, a category). For questionnaires, include the name of the questionnaires, scale values (e.g., Likert scale from 1 to 5, with 1 =… , 2 = …), provide examples of questions. Always cite the original creator of the questionnaire. Provide psychometric data of questionnaires if available in previous work.


Statistical analysis

Program
Indicate the program and the version of the program you plan to use for your analyses. You can use any program you want, including SPSS and R. It is likely that all of you will use SPSS, but I can also guide you through analyses in other software.


Power
Execute and report a power analysis. This is an important step at this stage. You can use G*Power software. Provide a screenshot of the output you got.


Analysis
Indicate which statistical tests you will use, and describe the outcomes that would confirm or reject your hypothesis. The statistical test you choose has to be able to answer your hypothesis. If you are in doubt, reach out - or change your research question.
It is possible your research question may need a statistical method you are not yet familiar with. In that case you have to change your research question. Be mindful of the questions that can be answered with your current statistical knowledge. It is always better to have correct but simple analyses instead of incorrect but complicated ones.

title: 2  Proposal

Use the standard formatting: APA-style, Times New Roman, 12-point font, line spacing 2.0. Include page numbers.

What to Include in Thesis-related Emails?
It is important to include as much detail as possible so that the back-and-forth exchange is limited and you get an adequate response as soon as possible.
For example, if your question is related to certain sections, for each section you can include:

Introduction: relevant context, references, what you already have, what you need…
Methods: what you have done so far, what options you considered…
Results: what you want to achieve, what you did to get there, what you would like me to do to help you…
Discussion: relevant context, references, arguments you are unsure about…

This list is not exhaustive, and can vary per needs. However, in all thesis-related exchanges make sure to highlight what you have tried so far and what you need help with. If you have not tried anything yet, it is likely my response would not be sufficient to solve your problem.


Contact Frequency

Thesis-related
To ensure fairness, there is a limited amount of times you can contact me for urgent, thesis-related matters.

Urgent means that it cannot wait until the next meeting/feedback point.
Thesis-related means that it has to do with a certain section of the thesis, the thesis process, thesis rules, etc. Almost all information you might need is freely available to you on Canvas or on this website.

For this type of contact, you can contact me up to 6-7 times. Do know that I will not be counting these emails unless I notice a disproportionate amount of contact points*.
* A contact point refers to the entire email exchange. If my response is not clear, please feel free to ask for clarification. This is not considered a separate contact point.


Not thesis-related
Please note that there are no limits on emails that have to do with e.g., booking a meeting, personal issues (such as sickness, family issues, mental health issues,…), procedural issues (e.g., if you cannot open a link on this website). You are free to contact me whenever.



Reply frequency
The supervision time allocated to me is limited. This means that apart from supervision, I have additional responsibilities with their own deadlines. Therefore, you can expect to receive a reply any time within 5 working days*. I will likely reply a lot sooner, but keep this in mind when planning your work. For example, if you only start working on a section a few days before the deadline and get stuck, it is possible you will not be able to get help on time.
* If it has been longer than this, and I am not on holiday, please send me a reminder. However, sending reminders too early is prohibited and could affect your final thesis grade (namely, the work attitude section in the rubric).

title: FAQ
section: How much time should I spend on my thesis?
text:
How much time should I spend on my thesis?
      
    
    
      
        Bachelor's thesis in this program is worth 12 ECTS. This is equivalent to 336 hours of work. This averages to about 16 hours per week for the entire thesis period. It is very likely that you will need less time. At the same time, it is also likely that you will have weeks where you are spending less time on the thesis (e.g., during exam weeks, while waiting for feedback, etc.). Therefore, it is important to be mindful of the time you have available per week in order to successfully complete this project.
      
    
  
  
    
      
        I heard from my friends that they are doing something differently. Why are we not expected to do it the same way?
      
    
    
      
        A thesis project, and generally any scientific project, does not have one way of being done. There are many valid, acceptable, and evidence-supported approaches that can be taken depending on both needs of the project and the supervisor's preferred way of working. If you believe something can be done better, I am very happy to learn about your idea and potentially integrate it! A thesis project is a two-way street, so in the end both you and I will learn something new from it.
      
    
  
    
    
      
        What if I am running out of time, and can see that I will not be able to submit a section by the agreed deadline?
      
    
    
      
        If this is just about a thesis section (e.g., introduction, methods, ...) and NOT the final, official product, please let me know ASAP about your delay. It is perfectly normal to have off-days or weeks, and realizing you need a bit more time because of it. I am very happy to work with you to make this work, however, I can only do so if you let me know about your delay on time. 
        For example, if you are three days away from the deadline, and know that there is no way you will be done on time, you should let me know. Generally, it is fine to be a day or two late, and I will not penalize you for this (i.e., it will not affect your process grade) if you communicated it promptly. However, being late does mean you might get feedback later, since I plan time for going over submissions and it is often very soon after the deadline.

title: FAQ
text:
Content

  
    
      
        How many references should I include in my thesis?
      
    
    
      
        This is a very common question, and it is one that (unfortunately for you) does not have an answer. In my bachelor's thesis I included 71, but I have read theses that included anywhere from 25 to 100+. The number of references does not provide any indication for the quality of the written work. However, lack of references can lead to plagiarism, unsupported claims, weak arguments, and worse final evaluation. Therefore, always remember to provide references for all of the claims/arguments you make, even if it is something you consider general knowledge.

title: FAQ
text:
Special circumstances

  
    
      
        What if I have to hand in my final thesis later?
      
    
    
      
        For this, you have to contact the examination board at examinationboardtsb@tilburguniversity.edu. Neither me, nor the thesis coordinator, can allow you to hand your work in late, nor can we push the final deadline. It is up to the examination board to make this call. However, you are free to contact me for advice on this matter.
